newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-South African banks aim to lure black savings.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-South African banks aim to lure black savings.

text.p: South African banks are trying out a wide range of ideas including cash prizes and free life insurance to attract savings deposits from the country's black majority.
They are naturally limited by the fact that many black South Africans are eking out a subsistence living and are more likely to need loans than to become substantial savers.
But efforts to draw black South Africans into the formal banking net have resulted in the development of innovative savings and lending products by a spate of new niche banks.
These have included Cashbank, Future Bank, New Bank People's Bank, Community Bank and E-Bank, to name but a few.
Some are offshoots of mainstream banks but others, like Cashbank, are former non-governmental organisations (NGOs) that have developed into financial institutions in their own right.

Not all have succeeded. Community Bank was put into curatorship earlier in 1996 after a liquidity crunch and has now been taken over by Unibank. E-Bank has been merged into Standard Bank Investment Corp Ltd's normal operations.
Community Bank's problems have been blamed on trying to run before it could walk and opening far too many branches on a limited capital base.

E-Bank was a victim of political correctness and the feeling that "separate products for the mass market are certainly not the way to go...it was regarded as being discriminatory by some people," according to a Standard Bank spokesman.
POOR SAVINGS RECORD
Most black South Africans have a poor savings record.

University of the Witwatersrand economics professor Harry Zarenda said: "Obviously we are not doing enough to generate savings, but the counter to that argument is that until unemployment problems start solving themselves and steady income growth becomes a pattern of wage growth, it is a chicken-and-egg situation."
But sizeable numbers of black South Africans are formally employed or self-employed and banks are introducing a range of innovative investment products which are often payroll-linked.

These products are sometimes linked to loans, cash prizes for regular savers, education or retrenchment insurance, free life insurance or schemes to ensure that savings are built up for the festive season.
Their target market is low-income earners pulling in a monthly salary of between 1,800 and 3,500 rand ($385-748) a month.

Some banks, however, have started demanding minimum deposits of 1,000 rand ($214) for group or club accounts because administering small savings accounts is expensive -- defeating the purpose of savings accounts for the poor.
Deloitte & Touche development finance expert Gabriel Davel said that most banks were not providing the right type of product for this market.
As a result, small savings accounts were expensive to administer and some banks were now trying to get out of them.

Davel said the banks would probably continue experimenting with various forms of savings accounts to widen their net of savers until one of them came up with a winning formula "and then the rest of the pack will follow".
INFORMAL SAVINGS CLUBS STILL POPULAR

Although the number of blacks using banks is increasing, most still save and borrow through the informal "stokvel" or savings club system, but Cashbank managing director Christine Glover said there was "room for us and the stokvels".

"In a lot of countries where there is low employment but high self-employment, saving often outstrips borrowing and there is no reason why over time we should not move in the same direction, Glover said.
"I think that there is a whole cultural shift that we have to do and how long that takes I do not know...it has started, but it will still take some years," she added.
